turns.prompt_text: I really need to be able to automate using a browser. Google Chrome I think is a good way to do it unless there really are a better. I don't know how much better Safari is but I have all my accounts logged in on Google Chrome I've realized that injecting JavaScript directly into the console seems to be the best way of interacting with Google Chrome. In order to do this, I imagine programmatically the easiest way to do this would be to have my Mac OS level script. Essentially a powershell script to do this
turns.response_html:
Injecting JavaScript is a solid instinct, especially when you want to bypass the "cold start" problem of logging back into accounts. On macOS, the most native way to bridge your system-level scripts with your browser is through AppleScript (which can be triggered from your terminal/shell scripts).

Since you are a software engineer comfortable with p5.js and CLI tools, here is the breakdown of how to achieve this effectively.

1. Enabling the "Secret" Bridge

By default, macOS blocks external scripts from injecting code into Chrome for security reasons. You must enable this once:

  • Open Google Chrome.
  • Go to the menu: View > Developer > Allow JavaScript from Apple Events.

2. The OS-Level Script (macOS "PowerShell")

On Mac, you don't use PowerShell; you use the Terminal (Zsh/Bash) or AppleScript. To run a script from the command line that talks to Chrome, you can use the osascript command.

Example: A shell script to click a button on the active page

#!/bin/zsh

# Your JavaScript logic
JS_CODE="document.querySelector('button.submit-btn').click();"

# Use osascript to tell Chrome to run that JS
osascript -e "tell application \"Google Chrome\" to tell active tab of window 1 to execute javascript \"$JS_CODE\""

3. Comparison of Approaches

While injecting via osascript is the easiest for existing sessions, here is how it stacks up against other methods you might consider:

MethodBest For...Cons
AppleScript / JXAAutomating your current window where you're already logged in.Harder to debug; limited to Mac.
Playwright/PuppeteerComplex, multi-step scraping or testing.Opens a "clean" browser (no logins/cookies) unless you point it to your User Profile folder.
Chrome ExtensionsPersistent UI changes or logic that runs on every page load.Requires a manifest file and manual installation in Dev Mode.

4. Taking it Further: JXA (JavaScript for Automation)

Since you are already a JavaScript fan, you don't actually have to write AppleScript. macOS has a "JavaScript version" of its automation engine called JXA.

You can create a .js file on your Mac and run it via osascript -l JavaScript my_script.js.

// Example JXA script
const chrome = Application('Google Chrome');
const activeTab = chrome.windows[0].activeTab();

const result = activeTab.execute({
  javascript: "document.title" 
});

console.log("The page title is: " + result);

Pro Tip for Chrome Profiles

If you ever decide to move to a professional framework like Playwright (which is much faster and more robust than AppleScript), you can actually tell it to launch your existing Chrome profile so you stay logged in:

const browser = await chromium.launchPersistentContext('/Users/yourname/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default', {
  executablePath: '/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome'
});

Warning: Be careful when using execute javascript with variables. If your JS code contains double quotes, it will break the shell command unless you escape them carefully.

turns.prompt_text: In my experience, playwright has downsides that it alerts the browser that it is being manipulated
turns.response_html:
You’re absolutely right. Playwright, Puppeteer, and Selenium all leave "fingerprints" that modern anti-bot services (like Cloudflare, Akamai, or DataDome) pick up instantly. Properties like navigator.webdriver are set to true, and the browser’s execution context often behaves slightly differently than a standard user session.

If you want to stick with your plan of OS-level injection into a standard Chrome instance, you avoid many of these flags because you are using a "braindead" browser—one that thinks it's just being used by a human, while AppleScript/JXA acts as a remote control.

Why Your Approach Bypasses Detection

  1. Genuine User Profile: You’re using your actual browser binary, extensions, and history.
  2. No navigator.webdriver: When you launch Chrome normally, this flag is false. Even when you inject JS via AppleScript, the flag remains false.
  3. Hardware Fingerprint: Automated drivers often use specific window sizes or lack GPU acceleration. By using your actual Chrome window, the hardware entropy (screen resolution, canvas rendering) looks like a real Mac.

Refining the "Stealth" Injection

Since you want a "PowerShell-like" experience on macOS to handle this, the best way to manage complexity is to create a Zsh wrapper. This allows you to pass variables from your terminal into the browser without messy escaping.

The "Chrome-Control" Zsh Function: You can add this to your .zshrc to make automation feel like a native CLI tool.

chrome-eval() {
  local js_code=$1
  osascript -e "tell application \"Google Chrome\" to tell active tab of window 1 to execute javascript \"$js_code\""
}

# Usage:
# chrome-eval "alert('Hello from the Terminal');"

The "Undetectable" Alternatives

If you find AppleScript too limiting for complex tasks (like waiting for elements to appear), here is how engineers usually solve the "Playwright is being detected" problem:

  • Playwright Stealth Plugin: There is a community-driven stealth plugin that specifically patches navigator.webdriver, WebGL fingerprints, and permissions gaps to make Playwright look "human."
  • CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol): Instead of AppleScript, you can launch Chrome with a "Remote Debugging Port" and connect to it. This gives you full programmatic control without the "Automated Test Software" banner.
    • Launch command: /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222
    • You can then attach Playwright to this already running instance. It’s much harder for websites to detect this than a standard automated launch.

Security Note

When you use execute javascript via AppleScript, you are effectively performing a self-XSS. Since you're working with your own accounts (which are already logged in), ensure any scripts you pull from the web are vetted so you don't inadvertently send your session cookies to a third party.

What kind of interaction are you looking to automate? If it's a "set it and forget it" background task, the AppleScript route is perfect; if you need to scrape data across 100 pages, the CDP/Remote Debugging route is significantly faster.

turns.response_html:
Combining these two routes gives you a powerful "Manual vs. Professional" automation toolkit. Both methods allow you to use your logged-in Chrome profile, but they differ in how they talk to the browser.

Route 1: The "Invisible Bridge" (AppleScript/JXA)

This is the most lightweight method. You use macOS’s native automation layer to "inject" code into your currently open tabs. It is virtually undetectable because you aren't using a "driver."

Step 1: Enable the Injection

For security, Chrome blocks external scripts by default.

  1. Open Google Chrome.
  2. Go to View > Developer > Allow JavaScript from Apple Events.

Step 2: Create Your "PowerShell" Wrapper

Since you prefer a CLI approach, add this function to your ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bash_profile).

# Open your config
nano ~/.zshrc

# Add this function
chrome-run() {
  local js_code=$1
  osascript -e "tell application \"Google Chrome\" to tell active tab of window 1 to execute javascript \"$js_code\""
}

# Save and reload
source ~/.zshrc

Step 3: Run Automation

Now you can trigger JS directly from your terminal: chrome-run "document.body.style.backgroundColor = 'red';"

Route 2: The "Professional Remote" (CDP + Playwright)

This is for complex tasks (waiting for elements, multi-page scraping). Instead of launching a "fake" browser, you tell your real Chrome to listen for commands via the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).

Step 1: Enable Remote Debugging

You must restart Chrome with a special flag. Note: Recent Chrome security updates (2025/2026) require you to manually allow this in the browser settings first.

  1. In Chrome, navigate to chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging.
  2. Check the box: "Allow remote debugging for this browser instance."
  3. Fully quit Chrome (Cmd+Q) and relaunch it via Terminal to open the port: 
    /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222

Step 2: Connect Playwright to Your Live Session

Instead of chromium.launch(), you use chromium.connectOverCDP(). This attaches Playwright to your existing window with all your accounts logged in.

const { chromium } = require('playwright');

(async () => {
  // Connect to your already-open Chrome
  const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP('http://localhost:9222');
  
  // Get the existing page instead of creating a new one
  const defaultContext = browser.contexts()[0];
  const page = defaultContext.pages()[0];

  console.log("Connected to:", await page.title());

  // Now use standard Playwright commands without detection
  await page.click('.submit-button');
})();

Comparison Summary

FeatureAppleScript (Route 1)CDP / Playwright (Route 2)
Setup Effort10 seconds2 minutes (requires port launch)
DetectionImpossible (Native OS event)Extremely Low (Uses real profile)
ComplexityBest for one-liners/simple clicksBest for logic loops & data scraping
UI ControlCan only talk to the active tabCan control any tab/window in the background

Recommendation for Your Workflow

  • For contract work "hacks": Use Route 1. It's fast and you can trigger it from a simple keyboard shortcut or shell script.
  • For robust tools/simulations: Use Route 2. Since you already use p5.js and node-based systems, having the full Playwright API (which is just a Node library) will feel much more natural for building complex automation.

turns.response_html:
You’re hitting on a classic engineering challenge: the "Cat and Mouse" game between automation and anti-bot systems. You are definitely not the first to realize that standard Playwright/Puppeteer setups are essentially "sending a flair" to the website saying, "I am a bot."

Because you are a software engineer with a background in cybersecurity and contract work, you’ll appreciate that the projects that actually work today are moving away from the "Automated Driver" model and toward your proposed "Live Session Injection" model.

Here are the specific projects and GitHub repos that follow your logic:

1. The "Native" Path (AppleScript & JXA)

Since you mentioned using a "PowerShell-like" script on Mac, this is your most direct route. There aren't many "massive" repos here because the code is so simple, but there are highly functional Gists and small MCP servers that bridge AI to your real browser.

  • Project: chrome-applescript-mcp (and similar AI bridges)
    • The Logic: This is a modern trend where developers use "Model Context Protocol" (MCP) servers to let tools (like Cursor or Claude Desktop) control their real Chrome via AppleScript.
    • Why it works: It uses the osascript command to "Execute JavaScript" exactly as you envisioned. Since it targets your running Chrome process, it inherits your login cookies, your specific hardware fingerprint, and your IP.
    • GitHub Search Key: Look for applescript-mcp or safari-mcp.

2. The "Stealth Driver" Path (Patched Playwright)

If you find AppleScript too clunky for complex logic, you should look at Patchright or CloakBrowser. These are "hardened" versions of Playwright that people in the scraping/automation industry use.

  • Project: Patchright
    • The Logic: It's a "drop-in" replacement for Playwright. You just change import { chromium } from 'playwright' to import { chromium } from 'patchright'.
    • Why it works: It modifies the Chromium source code (the C++ level) to remove flags like navigator.webdriver and spoof hardware details (GPU, screen resolution, etc.) before the browser even starts.
  • Project: CloakBrowser
    • The Logic: Similar to Patchright, but even more aggressive. It includes 30+ C++ level patches to Chromium to ensure the "TLS Fingerprint" (how your browser introduces itself to a server) looks exactly like a real user's Chrome.

3. The "Hybrid" Path (Remote Debugging Port)

This is likely where you will end up. You launch your real Chrome (the one you already have) and then connect Playwright to it.

  • Project: browser-act
    • The Logic: This project specifically manages a "persistent" Chrome profile. It handles the headache of starting Chrome with the --remote-debugging-port=9222 flag and allows tools to connect to it.
    • Why it works: It’s the "best of both worlds." You get the power of Playwright’s API but the "warm session" (logins/history) of your actual Chrome browser.

How to choose?

Given your interests, here is a quick "Decision Map":

If you want...Use this Project/Method
Absolute Zero SetupYour osascript idea (Route 1). It’s perfect for simple "click this, then that" scripts.
Complex Logic (Scraping)Patchright. It’s the standard for people who need to scale but are being blocked by Cloudflare.
AI IntegrationMCP-Chrome-Tabs. This turns your browser into a "skill" that other scripts can call.

My Recommendation

Since you’re already comfortable with the CLI, start by building a small Node.js CLI tool that uses Route 2 (CDP). It uses the JavaScript you already know, but connects to your live profile so you don't have to deal with logins or "Bot Detected" screens.
